title: The Primitive World: from the Refuge of Lausanne to the Egypt Found in a Deck of Cards
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Geneva, the rival birth and the name Corteiz
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and directly incompatible with the Nîmes stop below. Kept as a competing tradition rather than resolved. The Musée protestant notice, whose own title reads '1724 ou 1728', places the birth at Geneva in February 1724 and reports the precautionary registration name. Day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: The Protestant museum of France puts the birth at Geneva, in February 1724, and adds a detail no other account carries: the household enters the boy as Antoine Corteiz, a precaution taken because his father is a wanted man on the far side of the border. Antoine Court the elder has spent his adult life rebuilding the outlawed Reformed churches of France in barns and quarries and dry riverbeds, and there is a price on the surname. The notice that reports all of this is itself titled '1724 ou 1728'.
suggested_refs: The alias Corteiz, as reported in the Protestant biographical tradition
The clandestine assemblies of the Cévennes and Bas-Languedoc, the Churches of the Desert rebuilt by his father from 1715
sources: Musée protestant, notice 'Antoine Court de Gébelin (1724 ou 1728-1784)'

stops.name: Nîmes, the disputed birth
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and directly incompatible with the Geneva stop above. Lumières.Lausanne and the BnF authority record both place the birth at Nîmes around 1725, and the American Academy's membership page gives his dates as 1725-1784. Competing traditions give 1719 and 1728. No birth register has been produced by any source reached. Month and day default to 01-01 as unknown.
stops.campa: Against Geneva stand Lausanne and Paris. The university's biographical database and the Bibliothèque nationale both place the birth at Nîmes, around 1725, and the American Academy's membership page gives the same year. Older traditions give 1719, and 1728. Two cities, four dates, and no institution holding one of them will give way to another. No register has been produced that settles the question and none is likely to be, because the child of a hunted preacher is not entered in a parish book.
suggested_refs: The Churches of the Desert in Bas-Languedoc, and the warrant standing against Antoine Court the elder
sources: Lumières.Lausanne, University of Lausanne, biographical notice 43 (lumieres.unil.ch/fiches/bio/43/)
amacad.org, membership record for Antoine Court de Gébelin

stops.name: Lausanne, the family settles in exile
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by Lumières.Lausanne, which states that the Court family left France and settled at Lausanne in 1729. Month and day default to 01-01.
stops.campa: The Court family crosses out of France and settles at Lausanne, in the Pays de Vaud, where Bern's Protestant government tolerates what Versailles hangs men for. From here the elder Antoine Court runs the Churches of the Desert by correspondence, moving money, ordaining pastors and sending them back over the frontier to preach at night in ravines. The boy grows up inside an administration of the illegal, a house of ledgers and sealed packets and the names of men who cannot be written out in full.
suggested_refs: The Pays de Vaud under Bernese rule, refuge and command post of the French Reformed churches

stops.name: Académie de Lausanne, the encyclopedic formation
stops.date_confidence: attested as to substance by Lumières.Lausanne and the Musée protestant notice, which describe an education at the Academy given jointly by his father and the astronomer-mathematician Jean-Philippe Loys de Cheseaux. No start date is given in either; 1738 is an ordering placeholder inside the schooling years.
stops.campa: He is taught at the Academy and at home both, theology and philosophy and the classical languages, his father on one side and the astronomer and mathematician Jean-Philippe Loys de Cheseaux on the other. Neither of the Lausanne notices gives the year this begins. What they do say is that the education was encyclopedic, and they mean the word literally: grammar and prophecy and the motions of the stars taught as one subject, by two men who see no reason on earth to separate them.
suggested_refs: Jean-Philippe Loys de Cheseaux and the Lausanne scientific milieu of the 1730s and 1740s
sources: Musée protestant, notice 'Antoine Court de Gébelin (1724 ou 1728-1784)'

stops.name: Lausanne, secretary to Loys de Bochat
stops.date_confidence: attested to about 1743 by the Musée protestant notice, corroborated by Lumières.Lausanne, for the secretaryship to Charles Guillaume Loys de Bochat and the later increasing service to his own father down to 1760. Month and day default to 01-01.
stops.campa: From about his eighteenth year he works as secretary to Charles Guillaume Loys de Bochat, jurist and antiquarian, author of memoirs on the ancient history of Switzerland. The work is copying and indexing, and chasing Celtic and Roman survivals through charters and etymologies until a resemblance turns into an argument. Then, increasingly, he does the same office for his father, whose correspondence with the pastors inside France runs to thousands of letters, all of them to be copied out, filed and answered.
suggested_refs: Charles Guillaume Loys de Bochat, Mémoires critiques pour servir d'éclaircissemens sur divers points de l'histoire ancienne de la Suisse
sources: Musée protestant, notice 'Antoine Court de Gébelin (1724 ou 1728-1784)'

stops.name: Académie de Lausanne, the thesis on prophecy
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by Lumières.Lausanne, 'soutient une thèse de théologie le 4 juin 1754', corroborated by the Musée protestant notice. The title is commonly cited as De prophetiis; no copy of the thesis itself was reached in this pass.
stops.campa: On the fourth of June he defends a theology thesis before the Academy, cited ever after as De prophetiis, on the prophecies. The subject is not incidental in this house. His father's whole movement was thrown up out of the Camisard prophets of the Cévennes, shepherds and children who spoke in tongues and foretold deliverance, and the elder Court spent thirty years disciplining that inspiration back into consistories, synods and account books. No copy of the thesis has been located.
suggested_refs: De prophetiis, Lausanne, 4 June 1754, no copy located in this pass
sources: Musée protestant, notice 'Antoine Court de Gébelin (1724 ou 1728-1784)'

stops.name: Lausanne, ordained a minister
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by Lumières.Lausanne, 'Consacré pasteur en septembre 1754, C. devient lecteur au séminaire de Lausanne'. Day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: In September he is consecrated a minister of the Reformed church and made a lecteur at the French seminary. He is now qualified for the work the seminary exists to supply: crossing back into France under a false name, to preach to congregations that meet in woods and gravel pits, with a price on his head. Every other duty of the ministry he takes up. There is no record that he ever crosses. Whether he was never sent, or went and left nothing behind him, the Lausanne papers do not say.
suggested_refs: The clandestine pastorate of the Desert, the vocation the Lausanne seminary trained men for

stops.name: Séminaire français de Lausanne, philosophy, morals and logic
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the post by the Musée protestant notice, which gives philosophy, morality, logic and controversy at the French seminary; Lumières.Lausanne gives the teaching as ending in 1763 but leaves the start blank. The winter of 1754-55 is the Musée protestant's dating; 01 December is an ordering placeholder within it.
stops.campa: From the winter he teaches philosophy, morals, logic and controversy at the seminary his father founded, to young men who will be walked across the frontier when they finish. He drills them in how to argue with a Catholic curé and how to hold a syllogism steady under pressure. Eight years of it, winter after winter, in a lecture room a few streets above the lake. The register of the school is a list of future fugitives, and François Rochette, hanged at Toulouse in 1762, comes out of this network.
suggested_refs: The Séminaire français de Lausanne, founded 1729 by Antoine Court, training school of the clandestine French pastorate
sources: Musée protestant, notice 'Antoine Court de Gébelin (1724 ou 1728-1784)'

stops.name: Lausanne, the father's history of the Camisard wars
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by the Musée protestant notice on Antoine Court the elder, which records the 1760 publication of the Histoire des troubles des Cévennes and the son's assistance in preparing it for print. Month and day default to 01-01.
stops.campa: The elder Antoine Court publishes his history of the Camisard wars, the prophets and the guerrilla they made, written by the one man who afterward put the survivors back under discipline. The son helps prepare it for the press. It is the first time he handles a book that argues a persecuted people's case by assembling their documents in order and daring the reader to draw the conclusion himself. He will use the method for the rest of his life, on material his father would not have recognized.
suggested_refs: Antoine Court, Histoire des troubles des Cévennes ou de la guerre des Camisards (1760)

stops.name: Lausanne, the death of Antoine Court
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1760 at Lausanne by the Musée protestant notice and Lumières.Lausanne. No month is given in either source reached; June is an ordering placeholder and should not be quoted as a date.
stops.campa: His father dies at Lausanne, having rebuilt out of nothing a church the crown of France declared abolished in 1685. No office descends to the son, because the network was never an office; it ran on one man's correspondence and one man's credit with the merchants who paid for it. What comes down to the son is the address book and the unfinished business. He is nearly forty and has been teaching logic to other men's sons for eight years. No source reached gives the month of the death, only the year.
suggested_refs: The papers of Antoine Court the elder, now at the Bibliothèque de Genève

segments.name: Toulouse Answered from a Foreign Country

stops.name: Lausanne, Les Toulousaines
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by the Musée protestant notice and Lumières.Lausanne. The two Toulouse executions the book answers are attested to the day: Rochette hanged 19 February 1762 at the Place du Salin with the three Grenier brothers beheaded beside him, Calas broken on the wheel 10 March 1762 at the Place Saint-Georges. Court is not recorded at either. The stop is placed where he wrote, not where they died.
stops.campa: He publishes Les Toulousaines, fictive letters in defence of the Reformed religion, written against a single year in one city. On the nineteenth of February 1762 the pastor François Rochette was hanged in the Place du Salin, and the three Grenier brothers, Protestant gentlemen-glassmakers of the Comté de Foix, were beheaded beside him. On the tenth of March the merchant Jean Calas was broken on the wheel in the Place Saint-Georges for a son's suicide. Court is in Switzerland, working from letters. The book fails.
suggested_refs: Les Toulousaines, ou Lettres historiques et apologétiques en faveur de la religion réformée (1763)
The Place du Salin and the Place Saint-Georges at Toulouse, two squares and two scaffolds in three weeks of 1762
sources: Musée protestant, notice 'Antoine Court de Gébelin (1724 ou 1728-1784)'

stops.name: Lausanne, the departure
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by fr.wikipedia, 'Antoine Court de Gébelin', for the departure from Lausanne on 23 March 1763; Lumières.Lausanne independently ties the departure to 'l'échec des Toulousaines en 1763'.
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of March he leaves Lausanne. The Toulousaines has not moved anyone it needed to move, the teaching post is behind him, and the refuge that sheltered his family for thirty-four years has become a place from which nothing can be done. Voltaire has taken up the Calas case from Ferney, a day up the lake, and is proving in these same months that what overturns a French verdict is noise made inside France. Court goes to make it there.
suggested_refs: Voltaire's campaign for the rehabilitation of Jean Calas, conducted from Ferney, 1762-1765

stops.name: Nîmes, the Languedoc circuit
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Musée protestant notice gives the 1763 transition to France in general terms; no source reached itemizes the stages of a southern tour. Nîmes stands for the whole Cévenol and Languedoc circuit and the coordinate should be read as a region marker, not an address. Month is an ordering placeholder.
stops.campa: He travels through the Protestant south, the Cévennes and the Languedoc his father worked underground for forty years, meeting pastors, consistories and the notables whose money keeps the churches standing. He is seeing as an adult, and for the first time, the country his family is from, and he is counting while he looks: what a general settlement would cost, and who could be made to pay for it. No source reached itemizes the stages of the circuit, and Nîmes stands here for the whole of it.
suggested_refs: The consistories of Bas-Languedoc and the Cévennes, 1763
sources: Musée protestant, notice 'Antoine Court de Gébelin (1724 ou 1728-1784)'

segments.name: Paris, Agent of a Church That Does Not Exist

stops.name: Paris, arrival in October
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by fr.wikipedia, 'Antoine Court de Gébelin', and the Musée protestant notice, both giving October 1763 for the establishment in Paris. The first lodging is not identified in any source reached, so the coordinate marks central Paris. Day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: By October he is in Paris and will not leave it again for twenty years. He arrives as the unofficial agent of a church that legally does not exist, in the capital of the king whose grandfather abolished it, with no commission, no salary and no standing to petition anybody. The house he first lodges in is named in nothing reached. The strategy is the only one available to a man in that position: make yourself somebody whose opinion the capital wants, then spend the credit on toleration.
suggested_refs: The unofficial Protestant deputation at Paris, 1763-1787
sources: Musée protestant, notice 'Antoine Court de Gébelin (1724 ou 1728-1784)'

stops.name: Paris, the grandmother's name
stops.date_confidence: attested to about 1765 by the BnF authority record cb118979670, 'Autour de 1765, il ajoute à son patronyme Court le nom de sa grand-mère, Marie Gébelin'. Month and day default to 01-01.
stops.campa: He adds to Court the name of his paternal grandmother, Marie Gébelin, and from about this year signs himself Court de Gébelin. The extra syllables do in this city what a particle does. They make a Swiss pastor's son sound like a man with land somewhere. The plain surname Court belongs to the outlaw preacher of the Desert, hunted for forty years, and it is the wrong name to put at the head of a subscription list for a work of universal scholarship. He does not renounce the father. He annexes a grandmother.
suggested_refs: Marie Gébelin, paternal grandmother, whose surname became the second half of his

stops.name: Paris, the bank that never opens
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The scheme rests on the general biographical tradition of his Paris agency work as relayed by the Musée protestant notice; no prospectus, subscriber list or document of the bank itself was reached in this pass. Month is an ordering placeholder within 1765-1766.
stops.campa: He promotes a Protestant bank: the merchant capital of Bordeaux, Nîmes, Montpellier and Geneva gathered into a single instrument, lent to a crown perpetually short of money, and priced not in interest but in a legal settlement for the Reformed. It is toleration proposed as a financial product. The notables will not agree among themselves and the thing never opens. Twenty-two years later the Edict of Versailles will grant French Protestants a civil status, three years after he is dead.
suggested_refs: The Edict of Versailles, November 1787, granting non-Catholics a civil status in France
sources: Musée protestant, notice 'Antoine Court de Gébelin (1724 ou 1728-1784)'

stops.name: Rue Poupée, the first volume printed chez l'auteur
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by Lumières.Lausanne and the BnF authority record, both giving the run as 1773-1782 in nine quarto volumes. The rue Poupée imprint address is from a BnF/CCFr catalogue record cited in the dossier and not independently opened; the street ran between the rue de la Harpe and the rue Hautefeuille and was demolished in the 1850s, so the coordinate is approximate to its former line.
stops.campa: He publishes the first volume of Le Monde primitif, analysé et comparé avec le monde moderne, from his own address in the rue Poupée, in the house of M. Boucher, chez l'auteur. The thesis is that one primitive world underlies every later one, that its language, its calendar, its allegories and its games survive in fragments in every nation on earth, and that comparison can put the fragments back together. Quarto, engraved plates, sold by subscription, printed at the author's own risk and out of the author's own rooms.
suggested_refs: The rue Poupée, Paris, demolished in the rebuilding of the 1850s

stops.name: Rue Poupée, the natural history of speech
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by the BnF authority record cb118979670, which lists the Histoire naturelle de la parole among his works at 1776 and records a posthumous reprint in 1816 without publisher detail. Month and day default to 01-01.
stops.campa: He pulls the linguistic argument out of the larger work and issues it alone as the Histoire naturelle de la parole, a natural history of speech with a sketch of universal grammar. Language here is not convention but anatomy: the vocal organs can make only so many sounds, each sound carries meaning by the manner of its production, and every alphabet on earth is a diagram of a mouth caught mid-utterance. He is engraving throats and tongues in a book of etymologies. A reprint appears in 1816.
suggested_refs: Histoire naturelle de la parole, ou Précis de l'origine du langage et de la grammaire universelle (1776; reprinted 1816)
The vocal-organ and alphabet plates of Le Monde primitif

stops.name: Paris, the dictionary of Latin roots
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction to the year, from the works list in the BnF authority record cb118979670 for the Dictionnaire étymologique et raisonné des racines latines; the title page itself was not opened in this pass. Month and day default to 01-01.
stops.campa: He publishes the Dictionnaire étymologique et raisonné des racines latines, extracted from the Monde primitif and sold on its own. The BnF works list carries it at 1780; the title page itself was not opened in this pass. The method is everywhere the same. A word is broken back to a root, the root is matched to a sound, the sound is traced to the primitive world, and the resemblance is offered as the proof. Contemporaries who admire the erudition already notice that it will prove whatever is put into it.
suggested_refs: Dictionnaire étymologique et raisonné des racines latines, extrait du Monde primitif (1780)

stops.name: Paris, appointed royal censor
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by Lumières.Lausanne, 'nommé censeur royal en 1781 par le garde des Sceaux', and by the Musée protestant notice and fr.wikipedia. Month and day default to 01-01.
stops.campa: The garde des Sceaux appoints him censeur royal, an officer of the crown's book administration, empowered to approve or refuse what may lawfully be printed in France. He is a consecrated Protestant minister. His co-religionists in this kingdom still cannot marry lawfully, register a birth, or inherit without passing through a Catholic ceremony, and one of them is now paid by the monarchy to decide what the monarchy's subjects may read. He takes the office and goes on agitating for the settlement.
suggested_refs: The Direction de la librairie and the corps of royal censors under Louis XVI
sources: Musée protestant, notice 'Antoine Court de Gébelin (1724 ou 1728-1784)'

stops.name: Rue Poupée, the ninth volume
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by Lumières.Lausanne and the BnF authority record, both closing the published run at 1782. Older bibliographies count ten or eleven volumes depending on how bound sets divide the installments; modern catalogues normalize the run to nine. Month and day default to 01-01.
stops.campa: The ninth volume closes the published run, nine years and some thousands of quarto pages after the first. The plan had been larger. The primitive world was to be reassembled entire, grammar, mythology, calendar, blazon, coins and games, and what stands on the shelf is a torso. Older bibliographies count the set at ten volumes, or eleven, depending on how a binder divided the installments; the catalogues have settled on nine. Subscribers have been falling away for some time. He is still promising continuations in print at the end.
suggested_refs: Le Monde primitif, analysé et comparé avec le monde moderne, 9 vols. in quarto, Paris, 1773-1782

stops.name: Rue de la Bûcherie, received into Freemasonry
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and the date is contested three ways. BnF cb118979670 gives 'initié à la franc-maçonnerie peu après 1776'; en.wikipedia gives initiation at Les Amis Réunis in 1771; fr.wikipedia gives reception at Les Amis Réunis as associate member in 1778. The lodge address on the rue de la Bûcherie is the traditional one for the Neuf Soeurs and is itself uncertain. 1776 is taken as the ordering placeholder.
stops.campa: He is received into Freemasonry at Paris. The date will not hold still: the Bibliothèque nationale says shortly after 1776, the English account says the lodge of the Amis Réunis in 1771, the French says associate member of that same lodge in 1778. What is certain is the room he enters, where astronomers, sculptors and the correspondents of American rebels sit together under a discipline that outranks their confessions. For a Protestant with no legal standing in the kingdom, that room is a form of citizenship.
suggested_refs: The Loge des Neuf Soeurs, traditionally sited on the rue de la Bûcherie, Left Bank

stops.name: Rue de la Bûcherie, Voltaire conducted to his initiation
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by en.wikipedia, 'Neuf Soeurs', 'Initiated on April 4, 1778, in Paris; his conductors were Benjamin Franklin and Antoine Court de Gebelin', corroborated by Lumières.Lausanne for the 1778 sponsorship, and matching the canonical scene in benjamin_franklin.journey.json.
stops.campa: On the fourth of April, in the lodge of the Nine Sisters, Court de Gébelin and Benjamin Franklin walk Voltaire between them to his initiation. Voltaire is eighty-three and has six weeks to live. Sixteen years earlier the two of them had worked the Calas case from opposite ends of the same country, one with a book of letters out of Switzerland that nobody read, the other with a campaign out of Ferney that broke a parlement's judgment. Now one of them holds the old man's arm and the other holds the other.
suggested_refs: Records of the Loge des Neuf Soeurs, Paris, 1778-1781

stops.name: Rue Poupée, the letter to Franklin
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, downgraded deliberately. The letter is catalogued as Founders Online, Franklin Papers 01-26-02-0633, dated 29 June 1778; that page returns an empty body on every attempt made in this pass, the API endpoint returns nothing, and franklinpapers.org serves only a frameset. Content and signature line are carried as reported, not read.
stops.campa: He writes to Franklin as Secrétaire de la Loge des IX. Soeurs, inviting the American and his family to a lodge gathering at the Ranelagh in Passy, and gives his own address in the rue Poupée. The letter is catalogued in the Franklin Papers. The page could not be opened on any attempt made here, so the text is reported and not read. A refugee preacher's son and a printer from Philadelphia are arranging an evening by post, in the summer the French fleet sails for America.
suggested_refs: Founders Online, Franklin Papers 01-26-02-0633, letter of 29 June 1778, unopened in this pass

stops.name: Le Ranelagh de Passy, the invited evening
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The venue is firm: fr.wikipedia, 'Jardin du Ranelagh', records the petit Ranelagh opened 25 July 1774 in the gardens of the château de la Muette at Passy, and gives the present garden's coordinates, used here. The lodge event itself rests on the unopened Franklin letter, and no attendance is recorded anywhere reached.
stops.campa: The Ranelagh is a pleasure garden opened four years earlier in the grounds of the château de la Muette at Passy, made by Morissan with the Maréchal de Soubise's permission and modelled on Lord Ranelagh's rotunda at Chelsea. A ballroom, gravel walks, an orchestra, and the whole of fashionable Paris paying to be seen walking in it. Franklin lodges ten minutes away. Whether he came to the lodge's evening here is recorded nowhere that could be reached.
suggested_refs: The petit Ranelagh at Passy, opened 25 July 1774 in the gardens of the château de la Muette

stops.name: Paris, secretary of the lodge
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1779 by fr.wikipedia, which places him as secretary of Les Neuf Soeurs under Jérôme de Lalande's presidency; the BnF record and the Musée protestant notice give the secretaryship without a year. The 1776 date sometimes attached to the office is not supported by any source reached. Coordinate is the canonical central Paris pin used across this corpus for the lodge. Month and day default to 01-01.
stops.campa: He serves as secretary of the Neuf Soeurs under the presidency of Jérôme de Lalande, the astronomer who computed with Clairaut and Lepaute the return of Halley's comet. The lodge is a learned society that happens to wear aprons: Greuze, Houdon, Bailly, Franklin, and the widow Helvétius sending supper. It is the same office he held for Loys de Bochat at eighteen, in a larger room and better company. He keeps the minutes, writes the invitations, and stands at the door taking names.
suggested_refs: Jérôme de Lalande, Vénérable of the Loge des Neuf Soeurs, 1779

stops.name: Paris, the Société Apollonienne
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the constitution date, which is synthesized from Neuf Soeurs scholarship not independently opened in this pass; fr.wikipedia and the Oratoire du Louvre notice both attest his presidency of the learned society that became the Musée de Paris. The meeting address is not established in any source reached, so the coordinate is the canonical central Paris pin.
stops.campa: He presides over a new body constituted at the end of the year, the Société Apollonienne, for public instruction in the arts and sciences, soon reorganized and renamed the Musée de Paris. Anyone who subscribes may attend: lectures on chemistry, on poetry, on grammar, delivered to a paying room rather than to an academy of forty immortals. It is the Monde primitif turned into an institution, universal knowledge sold by the season. Where it met is not established in anything reached.
suggested_refs: The Musée de Paris, successor to the Société Apollonienne, and its public lecture courses
sources: oratoiredulouvre.epudf.org, notice on Court de Gébelin

stops.name: Paris, elected across the Atlantic
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year and class: amacad.org gives 'Election: 1781' and 'International Honorary Member', and nothing more. The day 22 August, and the acknowledgement letter of 24 January 1782, appear on no page reached and are treated here as unsourced. The American Philosophical Society election of 1783 is corroborated by en.wikipedia; as.amphilsoc.org returned 403. Month and day default to 01-01.
stops.campa: The American Academy of Arts and Sciences, founded the year before at Boston, elects him an International Honorary Member. Two years on, the American Philosophical Society at Philadelphia elects him too. A republic still fighting for its existence is assembling learned societies and stocking them with the Paris men its envoy dines with, and the envoy is Franklin. What the Academy's own record actually gives is the year and the class of membership. The day, and the letter he is said to have written back, are on no page that could be opened.
suggested_refs: American Academy of Arts and Sciences, membership record, election of 1781
American Philosophical Society, member record, election of 1783
sources: amacad.org, membership record for Antoine Court de Gébelin

stops.name: Paris, commissioner of archives among the Philalèthes
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The February 1781 appointment as commissioner of archives in the Philalèthes system under Savalette de Langes, and the later removal for absence attributed to illness, come from specialist Masonic scholarship (shs.cairn.info) that could not be re-opened in this pass. Day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: In February the Philalèthes, the higher-degree research system run by Savalette de Langes out of the lodge of the Amis Réunis, make him commissioner of archives. The Philalèthes are collectors: manuscripts, rituals, alchemical papers, the correspondence of every hermetic pretender in Europe, gathered on the theory that somewhere in the heap the true tradition is recoverable by comparison. It is the method of the Monde primitif applied to Masonry. He is later struck off the commission for absence, put down to illness.
suggested_refs: The Philalèthes archive assembled by Savalette de Langes at the Amis Réunis, and the conventions of 1785 and 1787
sources: Masonic scholarship reported via shs.cairn.info, not re-opened in this pass

stops.name: Paris, the game at Madame la C. d'H.'s
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The scene is known only from Court's own text, which dates it as 'il y a quelques années' relative to the 1781 printing; the address is unidentified and the coordinate is the canonical central Paris pin, a placeholder for an unlocated house. Secondary accounts render the episode only as 'a group of women playing cards' and carry neither the recently-arrived lady nor the quarter of an hour.
stops.campa: Invited to call on a lady of his acquaintance lately arrived from Germany or Switzerland, he finds her at cards with company, at a game he does not know. He casts his eyes on the pack. Within a quarter of an hour, by his own account, the game has been gone through, explained and declared Egyptian. No older deck is fetched down, nothing is compared with anything, no document is opened; the recognition is the evidence. The room stops playing and begins handing him cards, one after another, to interpret.
stops.quote: Invited a few years ago to go and see a Lady of our Friends, Madame la C. d'H., who arrived from Germany or Switzerland, we found her busy playing this Game with some other People... I cast my eyes there, and immediately I recognized its Allegory: each one to leave his Game and come to see this marvellous Card where I perceived what they had never seen: each one to show me another: in a quarter of an hour the Game was gone through, explained, declared Egyptian.
stops.quote_source: Court de Gébelin, 'Du Jeu des Tarots', Le Monde primitif, tome VIII (Paris, 1781), Article I, p. 367, verified against the 1781 first edition at archive.org/details/mondeprimitifana08cour; English is a modern uncredited translation, corrected here from 'this marvelous Map' to 'this marvellous Card' (cette Carte merveilleuse)
suggested_refs: Madame la C. d'H., unidentified, at whose table the tarot was declared Egyptian
sources: Court de Gébelin, Le Monde primitif, tome VIII (1781), archive.org/details/mondeprimitifana08cour

stops.name: Rue Poupée, the Egyptian book declared
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year: the essay 'Du Jeu des Tarots' appears in volume VIII of Le Monde primitif, Paris, 1781, at pp. 365 following, read directly in the Internet Archive scan of the first edition. en.wikipedia cites the essay at pp. 365-380; the dossier's 365-410 and 365-394 are not corroborated. Month and day default to 01-01.
stops.campa: Volume VIII carries the essay Du Jeu des Tarots. The argument opens as an announcement: a book of the ancient Egyptians survived the fire that took their libraries, is so common that no scholar has stooped to it, and has never once been suspected of being what it is. Seventy-seven leaves, or seventy-eight, in five classes. It is the pack that Italians and Germans have been gambling with for three hundred years, and nobody before him has tried to read a page of it.
stops.quote: The fact is, however, very true: this Egyptian Book, the only remnant of their superb Libraries, exists today: it is even so common that no Scholar has deigned to deal with it; no one before us having ever suspected its illustrious origin. This Book is composed of 77 leaves or depictions, even 78, divided into 5 classes... this Book is in a word the GAME of TAROTS.
stops.quote_source: Court de Gébelin, 'Du Jeu des Tarots', Le Monde primitif, tome VIII (Paris, 1781), section 'Ce Livre Egyptien existe', p. 365, verified against the 1781 first edition at archive.org/details/mondeprimitifana08cour; the original gives the counts as LXXVII and LXXVIII
suggested_refs: Le Monde primitif, tome VIII (1781), pp. 365ff., 'Du Jeu des Tarots'
sources: Court de Gébelin, Le Monde primitif, tome VIII (1781), archive.org/details/mondeprimitifana08cour
Michael Dummett, 'Origins of Tarot', New York Review of Books, 14 May 1981

stops.name: Paris, the Star read as Isis
stops.date_confidence: attested; the passage stands at p. 374-375 of the 1781 first edition, under trump N. XVII, which Court retitles La Canicule. Same volume and year as the stop above; the repeated date orders the reading of the essay and is not a separate event.
stops.campa: He goes through the trumps one at a time. Number seventeen, the card the makers call the Star, shows one great star ringed by seven smaller, a woman kneeling to empty two vessels, a butterfly on a flower. He renames the card La Canicule. The great star is Sirius, whose rising announced the flood; the woman is Isis, to whose kindness the flood was credited. Every element resolves and nothing in the picture resists him. He sets the verdict down in four words and moves to the next trump: C'est l'Egyptianisme tout pur.
stops.quote: The Lady who is below, and very attentive at this moment to spreading the water from her vases, is the Sovereign of the Heavens, Isis, to whose benevolence the floods of the Nile were attributed, which begin at the rising of the Dog-Star; thus this rising was the announcement of the flood.
stops.quote_source: Court de Gébelin, 'Du Jeu des Tarots', Le Monde primitif, tome VIII (Paris, 1781), trump N. XVII 'La Canicule', p. 375, verified against the 1781 first edition; English is a modern uncredited translation, corrected here from 'the rising of the Dog-Wave' to 'the rising of the Dog-Star' (le lever de la Canicule)
suggested_refs: The Star trump of the Tarot de Marseille, retitled La Canicule in Le Monde primitif
sources: Court de Gébelin, Le Monde primitif, tome VIII (1781), archive.org/details/mondeprimitifana08cour

stops.name: Paris, the High Priestess against the Popess
stops.date_confidence: attested; the passage stands at p. 370 of the 1781 first edition under the heading 'Grand-Prêtre & Grande-Prêtresse'. Same volume and year; the repeated date orders the reading of the essay.
stops.campa: Card five is the Chief of the Hierophants, card two his wife, and among the Egyptians, he notes, the heads of the priesthood were married. Then the argument that he believes closes the case: if moderns had invented these cards there would be no High Priestess in the pack at all, let alone one the German card-makers have ridiculously christened the Popess. The oddity is the proof. A thing this awkward cannot have been designed; therefore it is inherited; therefore it is old; therefore it is Egyptian.
stops.quote: No. V. represents the Chief of the Hierophants or the High Priest: No. II. the High Priestess or his wife: we know that among the Egyptians, the Heads of the Priesthood were married. If these Cards were the invention of the Moderns, we would not see a High Priestess there, much less under the name of Popess, as the German Card-makers have ridiculously named her.
stops.quote_source: Court de Gébelin, 'Du Jeu des Tarots', Le Monde primitif, tome VIII (Paris, 1781), section 'Grand-Prêtre & Grande-Prêtresse', p. 370, verified against the 1781 first edition at archive.org/details/mondeprimitifana08cour
suggested_refs: The Popess trump of the Tarot de Marseille
sources: Court de Gébelin, Le Monde primitif, tome VIII (1781), archive.org/details/mondeprimitifana08cour

stops.name: Paris, Tar and Ro
stops.date_confidence: attested; the etymology stands at p. 380 of the 1781 first edition under the running head 'Noms Orientaux conservés dans ce Jeu', sub-heading 'I. Tarots'. Same volume and year; the repeated date orders the reading of the essay.
stops.campa: The name itself is made to confess. Tar is way, or path; Ro, Ros, Rog is king, or royal; the word tarot is therefore pure Egyptian and means, word for word, the royal road of life. He knows no Egyptian. Nobody does. Champollion is nine years from being born and the Rosetta stone eighteen years from being turned out of a wall at el-Rashid. The etymology is produced by the same engine that produced the dictionary of Latin roots the year before, running now with no text at all to check it against.
stops.quote: The name of this Game is pure Egyptian: it is composed of the word Tar, which means way, path; and the word Ro, Ros, Rog, which means King, Royal. It is, word for word, the Royal path of life.
stops.quote_source: Court de Gébelin, 'Du Jeu des Tarots', Le Monde primitif, tome VIII (Paris, 1781), section 'Noms Orientaux conservés dans ce Jeu', I. Tarots, p. 380, verified against the 1781 first edition at archive.org/details/mondeprimitifana08cour
suggested_refs: Michael Dummett's demonstration that the Egyptian derivations of 'Tarot' are completely spurious, NYRB, 14 May 1981
sources: Court de Gébelin, Le Monde primitif, tome VIII (1781), archive.org/details/mondeprimitifana08cour
Michael Dummett, 'Origins of Tarot', New York Review of Books, 14 May 1981

stops.name: Rue Poupée, the second dissertation
stops.date_confidence: attested that a second, anonymous dissertation signed 'M. le C. de M***' is printed immediately after Court's essay in the same 1781 volume, and that Court announces it there in his own words. The identification of the author with the comte de Mellet is traditional attribution, not a signature: the text names only a general officer and provincial governor. Month is an ordering placeholder within the volume.
stops.campa: Printed immediately after his own essay, in the same volume, is a second one signed only M. le C. de M***, which Court introduces as the work of a general officer and provincial governor who honours him with his kindness. That dissertation supplies what Court's does not: the Book of Thoth, the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet laid against the twenty-two trumps, and a method for divining with the pack. Tradition gives the author as the comte de Mellet. Within two years Etteilla is selling the whole apparatus in the rue de l'Oseille for cash.
stops.quote: This Essay will be followed by a Dissertation where we establish how this Game was applied to the art of Divination; it is the work of a General Officer, Governor of a Province, who honors us with his kindness, and who has rediscovered in this Game with a very ingenious sagacity the Egyptian principles on the art of divining by Cards, principles which distinguished the first Bands of the Egyptians, badly named Bohemians, who spread throughout Europe.
stops.quote_source: Court de Gébelin, 'Du Jeu des Tarots', Le Monde primitif, tome VIII (Paris, 1781), end of the 'Division' section, p. 366, verified against the 1781 first edition; English corrected here from 'the first Bands from the Egyptians' to 'of the Egyptians' (les premières Bandes des Egyptiens)
suggested_refs: 'Recherches sur les Tarots, et sur la Divination par les Cartes des Tarots', signed M. le C. de M***, Le Monde primitif, tome VIII (1781)
Etteilla, Manière de se récréer avec le jeu de cartes nommées tarots (from 1783), and the Épître à M. Court de Gébelin (1784)
sources: Court de Gébelin, Le Monde primitif, tome VIII (1781), archive.org/details/mondeprimitifana08cour

stops.name: Paris, the letter to his subscribers on animal magnetism
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to publication detail. The 1783 Lettre de l'auteur du Monde primitif à Messieurs ses souscripteurs sur le magnétisme animal is reported by multiple secondary biographical sources; the Wood Library-Museum cataloguing page returned 403 and no copy of the pamphlet was opened in this pass. The illness is described in the biographical tradition as calculi. Coordinate is the canonical central Paris pin, also used in mesmer.journey.json for the Société de l'Harmonie universelle. Month and day default to 01-01.
stops.campa: Ill with what the biographies call calculi, he puts himself under Franz Anton Mesmer and then publishes the outcome: a letter to the subscribers of the Monde primitif describing his sickness, his treatment and his recovery, and calling for animal magnetism to be examined seriously rather than laughed at. A censeur royal, a member of two American academies, has put his name behind the tub, which is what Mesmer has wanted from a man of that rank for five years. No copy of the pamphlet was opened here; the cataloguing page returns a 403.
suggested_refs: Lettre de l'auteur du Monde primitif à Messieurs ses souscripteurs sur le magnétisme animal (1783)
sources: Musée protestant, notice 'Antoine Court de Gébelin (1724 ou 1728-1784)'

stops.name: Paris, the emptying lecture room
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The letter of 31 March 1784 is transcribed at French Wikisource, Lettres de Madame Roland de 1780 à 1793, letter 107, and the passage was read there directly. It is distinct from, and much better evidenced than, the later sexual allegation attached to Roland's name in the biographical tradition, which could not be located in any page reached.
stops.campa: Madame Roland writes to a correspondent on the last day of March that the museums are dying on every side, that Pilâtre has nobody at his lectures, that people of standing are withdrawing, and that only women and persons of no merit beyond their subscription still keep up Pilâtre and Cailhava and Gébelin. The public course was the last engine he had. He is fifty-nine, or sixty, or fifty-six, depending which birth is accepted. He has six weeks left.
stops.quote: Les musées se expirent de toutes parts; on ne conçoit pas comment Pilatre se soutient; il n'a personne à ses cours; les gens de marque se retirent; ce ne sont que des femmes et toutes personnes sans aucun mérite que leur contribution qui soutiennent encore et Pilatre et Cailhava et Gébelin.
stops.quote_source: Madame Roland, letter of 31 March 1784, Lettres de Madame Roland de 1780 à 1793, letter 107, French Wikisource
suggested_refs: The public lecture courses of the Musée de Paris in their last season
sources: French Wikisource, Lettres de Madame Roland de 1780 à 1793, letter 107

stops.name: Paris, death in May
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month and city, contradictory as to the day and left so. Lumières.Lausanne gives 10.05.1784 at Paris, at Mesmer's residence; the BnF authority record gives the night of 12-13 May 1784; fr.wikipedia gives 12 May, which is also the date carried in jean_baptiste_pitois_paul_christian.journey.json. All agree only on May 1784 in Paris. The day is set to 01 as an unknown, not as a claim.
stops.campa: He dies at Paris in May, at Mesmer's house or under Mesmer's immediate care, having told the reading public in print the year before that Mesmer had cured him. The Lausanne database gives the tenth. The Bibliothèque nationale gives the night of the twelfth to the thirteenth. Other traditions give the twelfth outright. Three months later the royal commission will report to the king that no magnetic fluid exists and that the cures are the work of imagination. The oval portrait by Pujos and Huot is engraved this year.
suggested_refs: The engraved oval portrait drawn by André Pujos and engraved by François Huot, 1784, Centre de recherche du château de Versailles

stops.name: Paris, the incompatible causes of death
stops.date_confidence: contradiction retained, not resolved. Lumières.Lausanne and the biographical tradition give calculi, consistent with his own 1783 pamphlet. fr.wikipedia reports an autopsy finding a carcinoma of the upper lip complicated by proteinuria. A venereal rumour is attached to Madame Roland's name in the biographical tradition and was not located in any page reached. No post-mortem report was produced by any source. The day is an ordering placeholder immediately after the death stop.
stops.campa: What killed him is not settled either. The Lausanne tradition and his own pamphlet say the stone. A French summary reports an autopsy finding a carcinoma of the upper lip complicated by proteinuria. A rumour of a venereal cause circulates under Madame Roland's name and could not be traced to any page reached here. Within days he is an argument rather than a man, the magnetiser's most respectable witness dead in the magnetiser's care. Stone, carcinoma, or the venereal rumour: no post-mortem report has been produced by anyone, and nothing reached decides between the three.
suggested_refs: The royal commission on animal magnetism, report of 11 August 1784

stops.name: Franconville, the tomb of the comte d'Albon
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by Lumières.Lausanne, 'Inhumé provisoirement à Paris, son corps est transféré le 10 juillet 1784 à Franconville dans le tombeau érigé par le comte d'Albon'. The coordinate is the Franconville town centre from fr.wikipedia; the exact site within the commune is not established, and the present state of the tomb could not be established either.
stops.campa: On the tenth of July his remains are lifted out of their provisional Paris grave and carried north to Franconville, where Claude-Camille-François, comte d'Albon, has raised a tomb for him. The exact spot inside the commune, park or chapel or open ground, is not established in anything reached, and whether the stone still stands could not be established either. He left no wife and no children; the Lausanne record lists him celibate. His papers, and his father's before him, go to Geneva. They are there now.
suggested_refs: The papers of Antoine Court and Antoine Court de Gébelin, Bibliothèque de Genève

stops.name: Paris, the posthumous sequel to the Rights of Man
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by the Musée protestant notice, which lists 'Devoirs du prince et du citoyen (posthume, 1789)' among his works. Whether the text is his, and in what state he left it, is not established by anything reached. Month and day default to 01-01.
stops.campa: Five years after his death a book comes out under his name, Devoirs du prince et du citoyen, offered as a sequel to the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. The Declaration is months old. The man credited with the sequel has been dead since before the Estates General were summoned, and spent twenty years in Paris asking a king for the civil existence of Protestants, which the Assembly granted in the same year without him. Whether he wrote a line of the book is not established.
suggested_refs: Devoirs du prince et du citoyen (posthumous, 1789)
sources: Musée protestant, notice 'Antoine Court de Gébelin (1724 ou 1728-1784)'
